title: Your Big Brain Wouldn’t Be Possible Without Sugar
gist: A short teaser on a Science analytical review from University of Sydney and University of Glasgow nutritional scientists arguing that glucose, not meat protein, was the binding constraint on hominin brain expansion across 4 million years of evolution.

insights.claim: A new analytical review in Science reframes the energetics of hominin brain evolution around glucose rather than the long-dominant explanation of protein from meat.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A carbohydrate-centric origin story for human cognition cuts against the paleo/meat-forward narrative that underwrites parts of the protein and low-carb food economy.
insights.quote: The focus on what fueled the evolution of our massive noggins has centered on protein from meat, but a new analytical review published today in Science is reframing the story around a much sweeter center: glucose.

insights.claim: Study author Jennie Brand-Miller says the brain's need for glucose has received little attention from anthropologists even though animal foods were important — an explicit claim of a blind spot in the field.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: When a field concedes a blind spot, expect a wave of follow-on publications and popular-science coverage reweighting carbohydrate's role in nutrition narratives.
insights.quote: While animal foods were important, the brain’s need for glucose has largely received little attention from anthropologists
insights.locator: study author Jennie Brand-Miller said in a statement

insights.claim: Hominin brain size quintupled over 4 million years, from about 300 grams in Australopithecus afarensis to about 1,500 grams in modern Homo sapiens, with metabolic needs rising in step.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The 5x scaling is the quantitative anchor for any claim about what diet could have paid for human cognition.
insights.quote: brain size of hominins quintupled from 300 grams in Australopithecus afarensis to 1,500 grams in modern Homo sapiens

insights.claim: The researchers modeled dietary intake against energy needs for varying brain and body sizes using primate dietary composition, fossil dental isotopes and morphology, and genetics — an energy-budget modeling approach rather than new fossil evidence.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Conclusions rest on modeling assumptions, not direct measurement — treat the glucose thesis as a strong reinterpretation of existing data rather than a settled finding.
insights.locator: Nutritional scientists from the University of Sydney
